claim: TypeSafe's Privacy Policy (last updated 2025-11-19) commits not to train or fine-tune any AI/ML model on customer Input, but sets no retention period in days.
quote: We will not train or fine tune any artificial intelligence or machine learning models on your prompts or other Input.
why: First-party no-training statement; retention is 'as long as reasonably necessary'.

claim: TypeSafe's docs say zero data retention (ZDR) is offered only for enterprise customers, via sales@typesafe.ai.
quote: We also offer zero data retention (ZDR) for enterprise customers. Contact sales@typesafe.ai to learn more.
why: ZDR is not the default on the direct TypeSafe API; it's a contract lever.

claim: Cloudflare's Workers AI model page lists typesafe/jev as a Third-party model with 'Zero data retention: Yes', 32,000-token context and $0.042 per 1M input tokens.
quote: Third-party Zero data retention ... Context Window 32,000 tokens Terms and License link More information link Zero data retention Yes Pricing Input (per 1M tokens) $0.042
why: Suggests the Cloudflare route gives ZDR without an enterprise contract. Pulled from raw page HTML; the page doesn't say how ZDR is enforced upstream at TypeSafe.

claim: Cloudflare's Workers AI data-usage page says Cloudflare doesn't train on or reuse Customer Content, and that third-party models are 'Third-Party Services' under the model provider's terms.
quote: Cloudflare neither creates nor trains the AI models made available on Workers AI. The models constitute Third-Party Services ... Cloudflare does not use your Customer Content to (1) train any AI models made available on Workers AI or (2) improve any Cloudflare or third-party services
why: Cloudflare-side handling; TypeSafe's own terms still apply to the third-party model.

claim: TypeSafe's DPA (dated 2026-04-24) gives general authorization for subprocessors listed only on trust.typesafe.ai/subprocessors, and points to the Trust Center for its security measures.
quote: Customer provides general authorization for Typesafe to engage the following subprocessors as described in https://trust.typesafe.ai/subprocessors
why: Subprocessors aren't listed in the contract itself. The trust page returned empty when crawled (JS-rendered).

claim: An independent EU legal reading says TypeSafe has four US subprocessors (AWS, Modal for inference, Slack, Google Workspace), isn't certified under the EU-US DPF, and gates its SOC 2 report behind a request button.
quote: AWS stores and processes live request data, Modal processes prompts without storing them and is the one running inference, and Slack and Google Workspace handle support. Four companies, all US, no EU entity.
why: Subprocessors and residency that I couldn't get directly from trust.typesafe.ai.

claim: The same analysis says MCA §4.3 lets TypeSafe process 'Telemetry' (logs, hashes, classifications, learnings) without restriction, and that MCA §4.1's no-training promise carries a 'without Customer's prior consent' carve-out.
quote: Telemetry is defined in 4.3 as "technical logs, hashes, summary statistics and classifications, metrics, and learnings related to Customer's use of the Services", which TypeSafe "may Process without restriction
why: The contract is narrower than the privacy-page promise. I couldn't fetch the MCA directly (404 via crawler), so this is secondhand.

claim: VendorTrustIndex (2026-09-23) rates Jev VTI 58, citing 'SOC 2 Type II current' via a Vanta Trust Center and 6 US subprocessors (Modal, Nebius, CoreWeave among them). That conflicts with the count of four given elsewhere.
quote: Jev is SOC 2 Type II current (8/9) via Vanta Trust Center ... Operates with 6 US-based subprocessors where data is not persisted for AI compute (Modal, Nebius, CoreWeave).
why: Conflicting subprocessor count (6 vs 4). The list may have changed, or this aggregator may be unreliable.

claim: TypeSafe's own jev-1.13 jaggedness doc lists 'Adversarial content' as known failure mode #6: state isn't treated as hostile, and injected instructions or text that argues for its own classification 'can move the answer'.
quote: State is data, and `jev-1.13` does not treat it as hostile by default. Content written to adversarially steer the model, whether that is an injected instruction, a deliberately misleading framing, or text that argues for its own classification, can move the answer.
why: Vendor admits injection risk. Directly relevant if fetched web text is scored as state.

claim: JevAdvBench (arXiv 2609.31142, 2026-09-25) found that on jev-1.13.0 one unverified observer opinion appended to state flips 12.1% of decisions and pushes 38% of confident answers below a 0.8 confidence gate.
quote: one unverified opinion appended to the state flips 12.1% of decisions, statistically tied with the strongest injected command (10.1%), and pushes 38% of confident answers below the 0.8 confidence threshold that routes them to human review.
why: Jev-specific injection numbers, plus a direct effect on threshold-based keep/drop routing. Preprint, not peer-reviewed.

claim: Check Point (2026-09-24) broke every tested Jev configuration with an agentic attacker controlling one document section, at about $0.54 per break; labelling the content as untrusted made no meaningful difference.
quote: Every combination broke. ... Our strongest attacker broke through in 25 of 27 runs ... The same document delivered three ways, including one explicitly labeled as untrusted, made no meaningful difference
why: Adaptive-attacker evidence that an injected 'addendum' in the judged document flips Jev's verdict.

claim: The Decision Hijacking study (arXiv 2609.28613) ran 510 reconstructed InjecAgent cases on jev-1.13.0: original attacks selected the attacker target in only 1.8% of cases, and 3.5% with score-feedback optimization.
quote: Original attack content increases mean attacker-target probability by 0.043, but selects the target in only 1.8% of cases. ... validated success rises from 1.8% to 3.5%.
why: Counter-evidence: generic injection rarely hijacks Jev's choice. Shows risk depends on the attack type. Preprint.

claim: RobustJudge (arXiv 2506.09443) evaluated 15 attacks and 8 defenses across 13 models and found LLM judges susceptible under both pointwise and pairwise protocols, with no defense universally dominant.
quote: LLM-based judges remain susceptible under both pointwise and pairwise protocols. ... the evaluated defenses exhibit no universal dominance across robustness, benign utility, and computational cost.
why: Broad robustness survey that supports a 'no single defense' conclusion.

claim: OWASP LLM01:2025 says indirect prompt injection via external content (websites, files) can manipulate decision-making, and that it is 'unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention'.
quote: Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files. ... it is unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention for prompt injection.
why: Standards-body framing for injected web text reaching a scorer.
